Antennas and arrays

Pattern to absolute gain

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how equal feed voltages combine into a directional pattern, and how that pattern acquires an absolute gain reference.

A satellite antenna must direct a finite amount of power toward its receivers. The complex array factor AF adds field contributions, including the geometric path phase k rₙ·r̂ and the feed phase ψₙ. Here k = 2π/λ, rₙ is element position in metres and r̂ is a unit observation direction. The exponent is dimensionless.

Fields add before power is calculated. The squared magnitude |AF|² contains the interference cross terms. Multiplying by an identical element power pattern Gₑₗ gives p(θ,φ), a relative intensity pattern. This product alone has no specified W/sr scale.

Integrate p over solid angle to obtain I = ∫p dΩ. Then U = Prad p/I has units W/sr and integrates to the specified radiated power Prad. Directivity D = 4πU/Prad = 4πp/I compares a chosen direction with the whole-sphere average. A zero rear hemisphere remains part of that whole-sphere reference.

Gain G = ηrad D uses power accepted by the antenna, with ηrad = Prad/Paccepted. Realized gain also includes port mismatch. Peak-normalizing a cut to 0 dB describes shape; it does not establish dBi. General synthesis can vary aₙ, but an equal-amplitude, on/off design changes active sites and phase instead.

Example

For one ideal element radiating uniformly into a hemisphere, p = 2 forward and zero rear. I = 4π, so D = 2 = 3.01 dBi forward. With ηrad = 0.8, G = 1.6 = 2.04 dBi. With 10 W accepted, 8 W is radiated and Uforward = 8/(2π) W/sr.

    Practice

    1. If all complex feed amplitudes are multiplied by 3, how do p, I and D change?

    Track the squared field magnitude in both numerator and denominator.

    p and I each multiply by 9. Their ratio is unchanged, so directivity is unchanged. Absolute intensity depends on the separately specified total radiated power.

    2. At fixed directivity, what happens to gain when radiation efficiency falls from 1 to 0.5?

    Use G = ηrad D and convert a power ratio with 10 log₁₀.

    Linear gain halves. Gain in dBi falls by 3.01 dB; the normalized pattern and directivity remain unchanged in this efficiency-only model.
